title: Is Gambling a Sin?
excerpt: Scripture never names gambling. It speaks of the lot, of the wish to be rich, of the household and the neighbor, and Christians who read it have reached two answers that have stood side by side for centuries. One question both must answer is who pays.
body:
A woman buys a lottery ticket every Friday with her groceries and had never thought of it as a moral question until a nephew home from a Christian college told her it was one. A man who teaches a Sunday class runs the office pool every spring, and would be surprised to hear that anyone minded. A young husband keeps an app on his phone for betting on games, and this winter he has begun moving money out of the account his wife thinks is for the baby. Across town, in the hall of a church that would never send a member into a casino, an older woman is selling raffle tickets for a new roof.

The skeptic has watched all of this and has a fair comment. Christians, he says, call the casino a sin and hold the raffle in the church basement. They frown at a poor man's lottery ticket and call a rich man's speculation good stewardship. And the book they appeal to never mentions gambling at all.

He is right about the book, and the rest of his charge deserves an answer more than a defense. Scripture has no commandment about betting. It says a good deal about the lot, the wish to be rich, work, the household and the neighbor, and Christians reading the same passages have reached two conclusions and held them side by side for many centuries.

Some readers come to this question because the betting has stopped being a question. The site's page on whether it is a sin [to drink, get a tattoo, or gamble](/help/is-it-a-sin) says it in one sentence: "When drinking or gambling has a grip you can't break, the question is no longer whether it's allowed." That page is the place to start, and [Find Help](/help) lists other places to turn. The argument below can wait. Nothing in this essay is financial advice.

## What Scripture Says, and What It Does Not

The Bible never mentions a lottery, but it mentions the lot often. Israel divided the promised land by lot (Numbers 26:55). Sailors in a storm cast lots, "and the lot fell on Jonah" (Jonah 1:7), and the apostles, choosing a replacement for Judas, prayed and cast lots, "and the lot fell on Matthias" (Acts 1:26). A lot settled what nobody could rig: "The lot puts an end to quarrels and decides between powerful contenders" (Proverbs 18:18).

Israel also said what it believed was happening when the lot was thrown. "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the Lord" (Proverbs 16:33). The Study Bible's note on [Proverbs 16](/study/bible/proverbs/16) draws the line that matters here: "The saying does not endorse gambling; it says that even outcomes that look random fall under God's rule." Chance in Scripture never has a will of its own. The Preacher who saw that "time and chance happen to them all" (Ecclesiastes 9:11) also wrote of "the work of God who makes everything" (Ecclesiastes 11:5).

Isaiah did condemn people who "set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny" (Isaiah 65:11), and the note on [Isaiah 65](/study/bible/isaiah/65) calls the two "gods of luck and fate." His quarrel was not with uncertainty but with people who fed it, as though luck could be courted.

There is one bet in the book of Judges, though the narrator draws no lesson about betting from it. At his wedding feast Samson put a riddle to thirty Philistine guests for a stake of "thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes" (Judges 14:12). When they could not solve it, they told his bride they would burn her and her father's house unless she got the answer out of him (Judges 14:15). She did, and he paid by going down to Ashkelon, killing thirty men and handing over their clothes (Judges 14:19). The narrator says God used the whole affair against the Philistines (Judges 14:4), and the Study Bible's note on [Judges 14](/study/bible/judges/14) is careful to call that "not approval of Samson's desires." It still shows what many later bets repeat. The people who paid for it were not the people who placed it.

What Scripture addresses plainly and often is the desire that sends most people to the table. "Those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction" (1 Timothy 6:9). Proverbs sets the fast fortune against the slow one: "Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it" (Proverbs 13:11). The New Testament says that whoever will not provide for his own household "is worse than an unbeliever" (1 Timothy 5:8). Jesus spoke of money as a trust: "if you have not been faithful in that which is another's, who will give you that which is your own?" (Luke 16:12). Over all of it stands one sentence: "Love does no wrong to a neighbor" (Romans 13:10).

## What the Church's Teachers Said

Christians have argued about games of chance since at least the end of the second century, and the early voices were severe. Clement of Alexandria, teaching in that city around the year 200, wrote that the game of dice "is to be prohibited, and the pursuit of gain, especially by dicing," and named the cause: "Such things the prodigality of luxury invents for the idle." A collection of church rules from the late fourth century, the Apostolic Canons, told any bishop, presbyter or deacon "who indulges himself in dice or drinking" to give it up or lose his office, and applied the same rule to lesser clergy and lay people. John Chrysostom, the preacher of Antioch and Constantinople, told his hearers that "it is not God that grants to play, but the devil," and complained in another sermon that in his hearers' houses "we shall find draughts and dice, but books nowhere, except among a few."

In the thirteenth century Thomas Aquinas quoted Chrysostom's sentence against his own view and answered that it "refers to the inordinate use of fun." The soul needs rest as the body does, he argued, and he told an old story of John the Evangelist, who was found at play with his disciples and asked an archer whether he could keep shooting forever. The bow would break, the man said, and so, John answered, would a mind that was never allowed to relax. Play, Aquinas concluded, has a virtue of its own. A lot drawn simply to divide something by chance, he wrote, "does not seem to imply any vice other than vanity," but a lot cast as an appeal to God when nothing required one "would seem to amount to tempting God." Asked whether winnings could be given as alms, he named the cases in which they had to be returned instead: money won from someone with no right to stake it, such as a child, and money won when a man, "with the desire of making money out of another man, entices him to play, and wins from him by cheating."

Among English Protestants the dispute turned on the lot itself. Late in the sixteenth century James Balmford, a minister who had taught on the subject in Newcastle, printed a dialogue against "playing at Cards, or Tables, or any other Game consisting in chance." A lot, he argued, is by nature an appeal to God, who decides it, and so belongs with the oath and with prayer, which no one may use in sport. Lots, he wrote in his own spelling, "are not to bee vsed either for profit or pleasure." Thomas Gataker answered in a treatise on lots that the scriptural lots through which God made his will known were extraordinary, and that "extraordinary examples make no generall rules." Balmford was still answering him in print in 1623. The Westminster Larger Catechism of 1647 leaned toward Balmford's premise. It placed lots under the third commandment, among the things by which God makes himself known that are to be "holily and reverently used," and under "You shall not steal" (Exodus 20:15) it listed "wasteful gaming" beside idleness and prodigality, among the ways people harm their own estate.

More than a century later John Wesley counted gaming among the ways a Christian may not gain at a neighbor's expense: "We cannot devour the increase of his lands, and perhaps the lands and houses themselves, by gaming." Christians today still divide along the line these teachers drew.

## The Case That Every Bet Is Wrong

Those who hold that gambling is wrong in itself, and not only in excess, make a case in four parts that is stronger than its reputation.

The first part concerns where the money comes from. Money changes hands honestly in three ways: as wages for work, as a gift, and in trade, where each side gives something and receives something it values more. A wager is none of these. By the terms of the game the winner's gain is the loser's loss, and neither meant the other to have it. Aquinas, in the same discussion of alms, recorded Aristotle's remark that such winnings are taken "from our friends to whom we ought rather to give." Paul told the thief to work "so that he may have something to share with anyone in need" (Ephesians 4:28), and a bet runs the other way.

The second concerns desire. The stake may be small, but what it trains is the hope that one evening can do what years of work have not. "Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have" (Hebrews 13:5). On this view the weekly ticket is a weekly rehearsal of discontent.

The third is Balmford's argument and the catechism's. If every decision of the lot is from the Lord, then to throw it for amusement or for gain treats his providence the way a man treats God's name when he swears by it in jest.

The fourth concerns the neighbor. In the help page's words, those who hold it "want no part in an industry that profits from people who can't stop." The person who plays for fun pays into the same game that is ruining someone else, and Paul's rule was to do nothing "that causes your brother to stumble" (Romans 14:21).

Its fear is a church at peace with a trade that lives off the weakest players, and believers who have learned to hope in luck. Its hard question is that no verse forbids a wager, and a prohibition built from these principles has to explain why it does not also forbid a farmer's planting, a merchant's venture and every kind of insurance, each of which stakes something on an outcome nobody controls.

## The Case for Freedom Within Limits

Those who hold that a wager can be a matter of freedom are not defending a habit or a debt. They hold that a small stake a person can afford, placed for the pleasure of the game, is not a sin, and their case also has four parts.

The first is that Scripture does not forbid it, and that a church which adds a rule God did not give has done what Scripture warns against. "For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1).

The second is that uncertainty runs through ordinary life, and Scripture treats living with it as part of being a creature. The farmer is told to sow morning and evening, "for you do not know which will prosper, this or that" (Ecclesiastes 11:6). James does not forbid the merchant his year of trade. He rebukes the boast and tells him to say, "If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that" (James 4:15). On this view the moral question is never whether there is risk, but what is staked, whose it is, and why.

The third is that rest and play are among God's gifts. Paul calls God the one "who richly provides us with everything to enjoy" (1 Timothy 6:17), and Gataker argued that light matters suit the lot best. In the help page's words, a little money put on a game among friends is "spending on entertainment, no different in principle from a ballgame ticket." The money lost is the price of an evening.

The fourth is that the sins are specific and have names: greed, deceit, theft, a household neglected, a neighbor harmed. Aquinas named cheating, enticing, and winning from those who could not consent. Westminster named waste. On this view those are the lines, and they are firm.

Its fear is a rule that never reaches the heart, and a church that condemns a widow's ticket and never asks how its own members invest. Its hard question is the one the stricter side presses hardest: where the money goes, and whose it was before it got there.

## Who Pays for It

That question is where the two cases meet, and part of it has an answer that takes no side.

Between friends at a kitchen table the losers pay the winners, and next week it may go the other way. A commercial game is different in kind. It is built so that the house keeps a share of every stake, so over time the players taken together lose more than they win. That is not an accusation; no game could stay open on any other terms. It follows that the house's income comes most of all from those who play most, and some of those are the people who cannot stop.

Then there are those who never placed a bet. Samson's wager was paid for by a frightened bride and thirty men who had never heard the riddle. The modern versions are less violent and far more common: a spouse who finds the savings gone, children whose needs wait behind the next stake, a friend whose loan will not come back. Aquinas and Wesley needed no verse that named gambling to see that someone was being hurt.

We have to stand inside this paragraph. Many of us belong to churches that have raised money with raffles and bingo nights and never asked whose money it was. Many of us have spoken of the lottery as a sin of the poor and of speculation as the prudence of the comfortable. The skeptic noticed, and he was right to.

## When It Has a Grip

For some readers none of this is about freedom. One of the signs the help page lists is this: "You bet to win back losses, hide how much you've spent, or borrow to keep playing." Scripture knows the condition: "whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved" (2 Peter 2:19). The page's counsel is direct: "For gambling, ask your doctor or a licensed counselor for someone who treats gambling problems, and if it has left you in debt, see [our page on money](/help/money)." [Find Help](/help) has the rest. This essay can't counsel anyone, and it is not financial or medical advice.

For the family the page has one more sentence: "And if the person you're helping can't stop, set the theology aside for now. They need help finding help." The promise to the one who is trapped is not that he will win the argument, but this: "So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed" (John 8:36).

## What Both Sides Hold

Some of this is settled among Christians who disagree about the rest. Greed is sin at any stake. Cheating is theft. Staking what the household needs is wrong, and so is drawing another person into a game in order to take his money. Chasing losses, hiding them and borrowing to play are, in the help page's words, "signs of a grip that needs help, not a debate." And every Christian owes love to his neighbor, including the one across the table.

Whether a Christian may ever place a small bet he can afford is a question of the third order. Faithful Christians have answered it both ways for many centuries, Scripture does not settle it with a verse, and this essay takes no side. The essay on [whether Christians should drink](/writing/should-christians-drink-alcohol) reads the chapter Paul wrote for disputes of this kind, and the essay on [the love of money](/writing/is-money-the-root-of-all-evil) takes up debt, contentment and giving.

Every Gospel records the lots at the cross, and Luke sets them beside a prayer. Jesus prayed, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do," and Luke adds in the same breath, "And they cast lots to divide his garments" (Luke 23:34). Some early manuscripts lack the prayer, as the note on [Luke 23](/study/bible/luke/23) says, but in the text most Bibles print, the soldiers were playing for the clothes of the man who was praying for them. John says they cast lots for the seamless tunic "to see whose it shall be," and that even this fulfilled a psalm (John 19:24); the note on [John 19](/study/bible/john/19) adds that "nothing in the passion is outside God's purpose." The lot was in God's hand that afternoon, as Proverbs says every lot is. It gave one soldier a tunic.

Scripture has not told the woman at the grocery counter, the man with the office pool, the young husband or the woman selling raffle tickets exactly where the line falls, and neither has this essay. It has told them who decides the lot, and who else is sitting at the table. And it has told them about one afternoon when lots were cast at the foot of a cross, and the one who paid had placed no bet.

*"The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the Lord."* (Proverbs 16:33)

*"Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have."* (Hebrews 13:5)
